chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Zurara, from Sama'ah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding the single leg, half the wergild; and regarding the ear, half the wergild when it is cut off from its root, and when its tip is cut, then in it is the value of a just person; and regarding the nose, when it is cut, the complete wergild; and regarding the back, when it breaks until its owner cannot discharge semen, the complete wergild; and regarding the manhood, when it is cut, the complete wergild; and regarding the tongue, when it is cut, the complete wergild.

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Wergild or blood money compensation for injury or death
key_terms.الظَّهْر: The back (specifically referring to the spine area in this context)
key_terms.قِيمَةُ عَدْلٍ: The value of a just person (a specific monetary valuation)

ai.seo_question: What is the blood money (diyah) for cutting off a leg, ear, nose, or tongue according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the foundational principles of *diyah* (blood money) by categorizing injuries based on their impact on bodily function and completeness, a classification system central to Shia fiqh. It specifically highlights the jurisprudential distinction where severing an ear from its root or a single leg incurs half the wergild, whereas injuries to the nose, back, tongue, or manhood trigger the full compensation, reflecting the severity of the loss. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on precise anatomical and functional assessment in determining financial liability for bodily harm.
